newsitem.title: USA: Tosco sees $40 mln profit from Pa. refinery.
newsitem.headline: Tosco sees $40 mln profit from Pa. refinery.

text.p: Tosco Corp's chief executive Thomas O'Malley said its soon-to-be revived Marcus Hook, Pennsylvania refinery is one of the brighest hopes for increased Tosco profits during the next two years.

"We would like to see it deliver $40 million pretax (profits) to this company beginning in July 1997," O'Malley told Reuters after delivering a luncheon speech to the annual Pacesetters Energy Conference here.
Tosco has said the refinery, near Philadelphia, had been losing money under the previous owner, BP America, the U.S. subsidiary of British Petroleum Co Plc.
Tosco bought the plant from BP last February.
O'Malley also told Reuters that he expected the plant to be every bit as profitable as its Bayway refinery near Linden, New Jersey, the largest refinery on the East Coast.
Asked if the Marcus Hook plant would cut into profits (per barrel) from its sister Bayway refinery, he said: "Marcus Hook will only cannibalize imports of refined products."

"We're only one-third (gasoline) self-sufficient on the East Coast," he said, referring to the region's dependence on oil products from "Refinery Row" on the U.S. Gulf Coast, plus imports from Latin America and Europe.
Tosco is considered by many Wall Street analysts as the Cadillac of independent refiners because of its high profitability and keen eye for bargain basement acquisitions.

Asked about future acquisitions, O'Malley said Tosco was still on the prowl for more refining assets, but would focus its search on the East and West Coasts, while ignoring possibility on the Gulf Coast.
The populous East and West Coasts both have easy access to water-borne crude shipments, O'Malley said.
"We could buy another five refineries on the Gulf Coast tomorrow. But it's not good capacity, it's not well located and not good for us. We're East Coast/West Coast kinds of guys," O'Malley said.

Tosco paid an estimated $60 million for the Philadelphia area plant -- renamed the Trainer refinery because of its location in a township so named. The deal came with rights to sell its gasoline under the well-known BP name at about 500 gasoline stations on the East Coast.
O'Malley said the refinery itself only cost $25 million.
"It is an extraordinary opportunity," he said, noting Tosco succeeded in cutting the refinery workforce to 350 from BP's previous payroll of 550.
BP mothballed the plant before transferring title to Tosco, after Tosco and the union representing workers failed to agree on staff reductions and on ending longstanding union work rules.
But Tosco finally struck a deal in August with union workers who agreed to come back to work rather than remain unemployed.
Tosco plans to reopen the plant next July after spending $50 million on a modernization project to maximize output of higher-value, light-end products like gasoline.
Tosco will process 150,000 barrels per day (bpd) of oil products, compared to about 180,000 bpd under BP.

The Bayway plant, Tosco's crown jewel in the New York City region, can process about 300,000 barrels per day of product, and has been called "the gasoline machine" by some oil traders because of its prodigious gasoline output.
-- Ransdell Pierson, New York Energy Desk +1 212 859 1620
